Four years ago Adan Matul was selling a Guatemalan sweet bread called pan de Xela out of a street cart in the San Fernando Valley. Now Matul and his family run El Sabor Auténtico de Xela a Guatemalan restaurant and bakery in Chatsworth.

“Everything we serve here is a reflection of our roots — the dishes our parents cooked what we snacked on the bread we had with our coffee” Matul told The LA Local. “We want our bread and dishes to evoke memories of home the warmth that we felt eating our mothers’ food.” 

The demand that led to El Sabor Auténtico de Xela opening its doors reflects a broader shift in LA. Los Angeles County is now home to the largest population of Guatemalans outside of Guatemala with more than 280000 residents as of 2025 — a roughly 35% increase over the past decade. As the community has grown so has the visibility of its food even as many Central American immigrants face increased immigration enforcement and political pressure.

Growing up Guatemalan American in Los Angeles I know that feeling. For years food from our homeland was hard to find — even in one of the most diverse food cities in the world.

That’s no longer the case.

Across LA dishes like pepián garnachas and tapado are moving from the margins to the mainstream. What was once hidden is now defining neighborhoods.

These five restaurants capture that shift.

By Andrea G. Mendez Ochoa for The LA Local

Los Angeles County health officials are investigating a localized outbreak of flea-borne typhus in Wilshire Center a dense area that overlaps with Koreatown.

The incident is the second reported typhus outbreak in the county this year and comes less than two months after health officials warned of the first outbreak in Pico Union. Out of seven people who were diagnosed with typhus five were hospitalized and eventually recovered according to health officials.

While the latest outbreak is in Wilshire Center the Department of Public Health says the risk of flea-borne typhus is countywide. The county has reported 109 cases so far this year.

Flea-borne typhus is caused by bacteria spread by infected fleas which can be carried by rats free-roaming cats opossums and other wildlife. People can become infected when flea feces enter cuts or scrapes or come into contact with the eyes. The illness does not spread from person to person.

The Department of Public Health is urging residents including those in Koreatown and surrounding neighborhoods to take steps to reduce their exposure to fleas.

One of most striking moments of Sunday’s record-breaking halftime show was when @badbunnypr dropped into his casita catching the family inside completely off guard. It was the first time anyone got to see inside the iconic set that first made an appearance last summer in his Puerto Rico residency.

The inside of the Super Bowl casita feels so much like a real loving Latino home because it was brought to life by a real Latino couple. Argentine production designers Federico Laboreau and Maximiliano Pizzi have been taking Hollywood by storm for years designing sets for film television and major live performances. They can now add Bad Bunny’s casita to their portfolio.

The couple also own Fuegos a speakeasy-style wine-bar and eatery in the Exposition Park neighborhood of South LA that makes empanadas sandwiches and asado.

For diehard Bad Bunny fans the casita is instantly recognizable echoing La Casita stage from his “No Me Quiero Ir De Aquí” residency a now-permanent fixture in his visual iconography that at the Super Bowl attracted celebrity guests like Cardi B Jessica Alba and Pedro Pascal.

Looking back Laboreau said the casita was one of the most meaningful experiences in his career.

“Other projects are nice portfolio projects but this one meant a lot not just because it’s the Super Bowl or Benito or the casita but because of the message” he explained. “It felt like I was showing to America that the Latino community has magic has love — and that we can do whatever we want.”

Long Beach firefighters doused a blaze that burned a homeless encampment on the Los Angeles River at Anaheim Street around 8 a.m. today. A single engine crew was able to quickly get the fire under control. No injuries were reported.

Around 250 people live along the 9.5-mile segment of the L.A. River that runs through Long Beach city officials estimated last year. Right now Long Beach's homelessness services bureau is in the middle of a two-year $17.4 million project ($11 million from a state grant) to try to house as many of them as possible.

In March they rented out the 60-bed Colonial Motel on Pacific Coast Highway and started moving in people from the river. The city’s goal is to move at least 50% of the people living on the riverbed and eventually funnel 80% of those into permanent housing. People in the program will also be offered drug programs job training and other services.

Despite plans like this homelessness has remained stubbornly high in Long Beach. In 2025 volunteers tallied 3595 homeless people locally a 6.5% year-over-year increase and the city’s highest total in more than a decade. The latest count took place in January. We've requested data from it which the city said they wouldn't release to us until later this month at the earliest.

High swells are hitting Long Beach again and weekend rain is on the way thanks to another hurricane. 

Waves arrived along the Peninsula on Wednesday — sending water onto the boardwalk and side streets — and returned Thursday slapping against the already weakened bulkhead that serves as the last line of defense for a number of beach homes.

With a coastal advisory in effect through Friday experts say 3-to-6-foot waves are being carried to shore by tides reaching 7 feet high and leaving behind dangerous rip currents.

Waves are being charged north by Hurricane Rachel which is expected to weaken considerably before it makes landfall 100 miles south of San Diego early Sunday and reaches the California-New Mexico border by Monday.

Forecasters say the system should still deliver heavy rain gusty winds dangerous surf and localized flooding with hazardous zones stretching as far north as Orange County.

In Long Beach rain could start as early as Saturday morning and linger through Tuesday night with the best chance from Sunday morning through Monday evening.

Totals are expected to be modest roughly a quarter to three-quarters of an inch with a small chance of thunderstorms. South-to-west gusts of 20 to 35 mph are likely from Saturday through Monday adding the risk of fallen trees and power lines.

“The wind would actually be a lot more problematic than the rain” said Long Beach Marine Safety Chief Gonzalo Medina. “You have a lot of trees already that we’re seeing just from this heat that have fallen. This heat has weakened the structure of a lot of these trees. And now you bring wind into the equation. The trees bring down power lines and it gets complicated after that.”

High tide hit around 10 a.m. today at the Long Beach Peninsula. Residents and city crews had been preparing for days with Hurricane Polo sending larger-than-normal swells our way Monday and Tuesday.

Residents said they expected the bulkhead to hold today but they anticipated more damage in the coming months as a potentially very powerful El Niño approaches. 

Earlier in September massive waves supercharged by Hurricane Marie battered oceanfront homes. Compared to that peninsula resident V.R. Venkataraman said “This is a walk in the park.” 

In recent weeks the city has undertaken stopgap measures: reinforcing the boardwalk and bulkhead and adding large sandbags to the bulkhead’s base. Yet residents said it isn’t enough. One bayside resident remarked that the sandbags have already diminished. Venkataraman called the reinforced bulkhead “a bandage on a wound.” Others remained skeptical that the beach could ever be rebuilt. The city says it's hurrying to start a $11.4 million dredging project to replenish sand on the beach and it's considering pricier long-term solutions.

“Owning a beachfront is a privilege” that comes with another fact of life Venkataraman said: “the ocean can come meet you at your home.”

Leslie Wilson and Janice Moultry used to come from Carson to walk on the beach they said. A month ago Wilson saw “sand. It was all sand. Now we see ocean” she said calling it the “new normal.”

The beach house at 5454 Ocean Blvd. in Long Beach has become a TV star but it's also got a rich history.

Built in 1939 for oilman Ronald Wayland Heath the house remained in the family for 82 years before hitting the market for the first time in 2019.

It was originally built on a pier — basically wooden stilts — that allowed waves to break under the house. That’s one of the main reasons it survived the Lash of St. Francis — the only tropical storm to make landfall in California in the 20th century. Several other nearby homes were washed into the water that day when nearly 5.5 inches of rain fell on the city combined with 65 mph wind gusts.

That left the original owner with virtually no neighbors. When the city brought in sand to broaden the beach the Heath family traded the land rights to the city in exchange for a vow from the city to never build anything in front of the house.

For nearly five decades Kim Dae-soon made Kim’s Home Center a little piece of home for generations of Korean immigrants offering familiar goods from Korea that helped them feel connected to the place they had left behind.

High tide hitting this morning at the Long Beach Peninsula. Residents and city crews had been preparing for days with Hurricane Polo set to send larger-than-normal swells our way Monday and Tuesday.

Residents said they expected the bulkhead to hold today but they anticipated more damage in the coming months as a potentially very powerful El Niño approaches. 

Earlier in September massive waves supercharged by Hurricane Marie battered oceanfront homes. Compared to that peninsula resident V.R. Venkataraman said “This is a walk in the park.” 

In recent weeks the city has undertaken stopgap measures: reinforcing the boardwalk and bulkhead and adding large sandbags to the bulkhead’s base. Yet residents said it isn’t enough. One bayside resident remarked that the sandbags have already diminished. Venkataraman called the reinforced bulkhead “a bandage on a wound.” Others remained skeptical that the beach could ever be rebuilt. The city says it's hurrying to start a $11.4 million dredging project to replenish sand on the beach and it's considering pricier long-term solutions.

“Owning a beachfront is a privilege” that comes with another fact of life Venkataraman said: “the ocean can come meet you at your home.”

Leslie Wilson and Janice Moultry used to come from Carson to walk on the beach they said. A month ago Wilson saw “sand. It was all sand. Now we see ocean” she said calling it the “new normal.”

Approximately 300 volunteers across 70 teams conducted a count of homeless people in Long Beach this morning.

Last year’s count identified 3595 people experiencing homelessness and data from Thursday’s count will likely be released in the spring. The data will be used to evaluate the effectiveness of Long Beach’s homeless services and help qualify them for grant funding.

A team of volunteers in the Park Estates neighborhood counted four unhoused people including Art a guitar player unaware of the Multi-Service Center the city’s hub for homeless services. He sleeps wherever he can find cover and added \"wherever I go I usually get chased off.” 

Volunteers deployed to the Westside north of the Port counted approximately 10 people sleeping on the street and at least double that number living in cars and RVs. Heather Filbey-McCabe a volunteer who works with Mental Health America of Los Angeles said she saw significantly more people living in makeshift encampments tents and cars in a nearby area last year — so many that her team called in reinforcement volunteers to complete the count and surveys. She said she was “shocked” to see far fewer this year. 

Nicolas Mendoza who emerged from a dumpster when volunteers arrived and joked that he slept on his bicycle the night before speculated that the streets were clearer because city officials had recently collected identification information from the neighborhood’s unhoused population in an attempt to get them into housing. 

Todd McQuiddy a 70-year-old auto-body-shop worker said his path to homelessness began with divorce. Now he lives in cars finding community with his five cats and people sleeping in the area. “This block is a tight group” he said. When volunteers arrived he had just returned from Jack in the Box with breakfast sandwiches for two friends who had spent the night on the sidewalk. 

One woman age 65 said she lost housing after her grandson died by suicide. She had been a substance abuse counselor but could not continue that work because she uses cannabis she said. Though she’s looked into shelters “everyone is full” she said."

The World Famous VIP Records sign will soon return to the public eye following approval by the Long Beach City Council to refurbish and reinstall it at a small park planned to be named for the historic landmark.

Council members voted unanimously Tuesday to spend up to $23500 to repair the sign which has deteriorated since it was put in storage in 2018.

Long Beach will also pay VIP Records $170000 in licensing fees to display its sign on city property for the next 5 years. Regular maintenance will be paid for by the city while profits from agreements to sublicense the name and logo will be split 50-50 between both parties.

Even as the sign sits in storage tourists have come from across the world to visit VIP Records at its new location just around the corner from its original store.

The shop was always a community gathering place that nurtured young creatives helping launch artists like Snoop Dogg Warren G and the late Nate Dogg. Its notoriety only grew in the ‘80s and ‘90s when the sign was prominently featured in Snoop’s “Who Am I? (What’s My Name)” video on the store’s roof.

Street vendors have become a major talking point among local politicians. During this current election season gubernatorial candidate Steve Hilton held a press conference on a Westlake sidewalk accusing vendors of “killing small businesses in California.”

Vendors have also been a flashpoint in the Los Angeles mayor’s race since Mayor Karen Bass said they should not be allowed to set up in front of restaurants during a debate in August.

Both Bass and Nithya Raman have since laid out how they’d support vendors: Raman said she’d ensure vendors benefit from major events like the 2028 Olympics create special vending zones and bring state and county permitting closer in line with how vendors operate while Bass has pointed to the city funding that’s gone toward providing vendors with free compliant carts and assistance with permit costs. Street vending has been legal in Los Angeles since 2018 but the permitting has not kept pace with the tens of thousands of vendors across the county according to the latest estimates.

With their livelihoods up for debate The LA Local spoke to vendors across different neighborhoods and invited them to share their thoughts experiences and ideas. They told us about the decrease in sales they’ve experienced as foot traffic plummeted after immigration raids their desire for a simpler permitting process worries about affording healthcare and their wish for respect.

Jonathan Hale has been painting crosswalks at some of the city’s most dangerous intersections for over a year turning neglected streets into quiet acts of protest and prevention. That work led to his arrest last fall on vandalism — a moment caught on video that went viral.

“We’re arguing for a legal mechanism. “I think they see the momentum in the moment” Hale said about the city. “We really want this to be like an alley-oop for the city. But I think it’s going to be unbelievably hard. It’s going to require the coordination of so many different bureaucratic organs. But we want to do it.”

Rey the southern sea otter was not expecting to be a mom.

She was found stranded in July 2023 and deemed unfit to return to the wild. She's been living at the @aquariumpacific and recently was introduced to Sunny a pup who was found orphaned on Asilomar State Beach in February. Their bond was immediate.

They're now together as part of the facility’s surrogacy program. It pairs maternal-age female otters with young motherless pups who would otherwise not survive on their own. As a surrogate mom she’s teaching her adopted baby everything she needs to know to fend for herself.

Sunny and Rey cannot be released into the wild. Experts say both are already too used to being around people and lack the survival instincts to make it on their own in the ocean. High swells are hitting Long Beach again and weekend rain is on the way thanks to another hurricane. 

Waves arrived along the Peninsula on Wednesday — sending water onto the boardwalk and side streets — and returned Thursday slapping against the already weakened bulkhead that serves as the last line of defense for a number of beach homes.

With a coastal advisory in effect through Friday experts say 3-to-6-foot waves are being carried to shore by tides reaching 7 feet high and leaving behind dangerous rip currents.

Waves are being charged north by Hurricane Rachel which is expected to weaken considerably before it makes landfall 100 miles south of San Diego early Sunday and reaches the California-New Mexico border by Monday.

Forecasters say the system should still deliver heavy rain gusty winds dangerous surf and localized flooding with hazardous zones stretching as far north as Orange County.

In Long Beach rain could start as early as Saturday morning and linger through Tuesday night with the best chance from Sunday morning through Monday evening.

Totals are expected to be modest roughly a quarter to three-quarters of an inch with a small chance of thunderstorms. South-to-west gusts of 20 to 35 mph are likely from Saturday through Monday adding the risk of fallen trees and power lines.

“The wind would actually be a lot more problematic than the rain” said Long Beach Marine Safety Chief Gonzalo Medina. “You have a lot of trees already that we’re seeing just from this heat that have fallen. This heat has weakened the structure of a lot of these trees. And now you bring wind into the equation. The trees bring down power lines and it gets complicated after that.”

All of the occupants in one vehicle were killed the DA said. The victims included Asherey Ryan 23 who was 8 ½ months pregnant her boyfriend Reynold Lester 24 their 11-month-old son Alonzo and their unborn child Armani. The couple was driving to Ryan’s final prenatal appointment the release said.
Nathesia Lewis 43 and Lynette Noble 38 were in another vehicle on a shopping trip when they were killed the release  said.

“The jury agreed that this was no accident” said DA Nathan J. Hochman. “Linton’s actions left behind heartbreaking wreckage that looked like a warzone traumatizing survivors and witnesses. She also caused devastation in the lives of the victims’ loved ones.”

A federal judge ruled that Border Patrol agents continued making illegal stops and arrests after she ordered them to quit.

In a tersely worded decision unsealed Thursday morning the judge wrote that agents had “again detained people without reasonable suspicion” relying on broad assumptions about day laborers instead of specific evidence of immigration violations.

The ruling by Judge Jennifer Thurston of the Eastern District of California grants a United Farm Workers motion to enforce a preliminary injunction the judge issued last year. That motion barred Border Patrol agents from detaining people in California’s Central Valley without documenting the specific facts and reasoning for the stops. According to one legal expert the ruling gives the Trump administration an opportunity to comply before consequences could escalate.

Thurston highlighted that point during a hearing last year telling the federal government: “You just can’t walk up to people with Brown skin and say ‘Give me your papers.”

Thurston’s original order also prohibited agents from carrying out warrantless arrests without first assessing whether a person is a flight risk.

Linguist Deborah Sanchez grew up hearing only a few words in Šmuwič an Indigenous language originating from the central Californian coast. Šmuwič words peppered her parents’ speech giving Sanchez glimpses of the language of her heritage.

Šmuwič exists in the family of Chumashan languages spoken across the region encompassing what is now San Luis Obispo to Malibu as well as interior land stretching toward the Central Valley. Approximately two centuries ago close to 90 languages were spoken in California then the most linguistically diverse area of North America according to the California Language Archive.

But for Šmuwič the last first-language speaker died in 1965. She left behind “remnants” Sanchez said — an archive of hundreds of recordings. Yet they remained inaccessible to the community for years Sanchez said. That began to change in the 1980s. A friend gave Sanchez’s mother a dictionary of 2000 Šmuwič words — part of linguist Kenneth Whistler’s dissertation — and she passed a copy onto Sanchez.

Now as faculty and a current master’s student at Cal State Long Beach Sanchez is devoting her life to stitching these words together revitalizing and sharing the language which has been dormant for decades. She sees it as “an ancestral responsibility to carry these things forward.”

Chef Marilyn’s restaurant is serving its customers again after a public dispute over legal ownership of the restaurant and brand.

Chef Marilyn whose real name is Marilyn Ann Cole reopened the restaurant last month after  temporarily closing its doors on April 20.

Cole opened her namesake restaurant on Crenshaw Boulevard 38 years ago. When the restaurant fell on hard times Cole said she struck a deal with attorneys Channing B. Smith and Cierra Carter in February to keep it afloat. Cole told The LA Local she didn’t fully understand the deal.

Smith and Carter denied any wrongdoing and explained in an Instagram post that they took steps to make the restaurant financially sound again when they entered into an agreement with Cole.

Cole regained physical possession of the restaurant in May but the attorneys’ publicist told The LA Local that although Cole had regained possession their legal issues remained unresolved.

The LA Local has reached out to Carter’s publicist for comment about the restaurant reopening.  Cole said she appreciated the community’s support and plans to continue strengthening her brand.

For years @uniondelbarrio has been patrolling the streets of Los Angeles keeping an eye out for federal immigration agents.

The group ramped up its efforts when President Donald Trump was sworn into his second term but when immigration raids surged last summer so did their work. Now the group’s morning updates on social media have become part of daily life for some LA residents almost akin to checking the weather.

The patrols are still going LA chapter founder Ron Gochez said because ICE has hardly slowed down. 

Federal agents arrested 1233 people in the region in September according to an analysis by The LA Local of the most recent ICE records obtained by the Deportation Data Project.

The total is about half the number arrested in June but three times higher than in previous years. 

Gochez and other activists believe those numbers would be even higher without the persistent efforts of volunteers to track ICE operations share legal resources and show solidarity with their immigrant neighbors.

“The raids are continuing the deportations are continuing and so we have the responsibility to protect our communities” said Gochez who served as a driver during an early morning patrol in December. “We’re happy that a lot more volunteers have been joining our efforts. Inglewood Unified School District announced it cleared a crucial state audit on Thursday taking it a step closer to ending its 14 years under state control.

The district has been run by a state-appointed administrator since it hit a financial crisis in 2012 with elected school board trustees sidelined to nonvoting advisory roles. It’s the longest such takeover in California’s history.

Now though the district could be just a year away from the school board regaining voting power and hiring a superintendent of its own choosing.

The state’s Fiscal Crisis and Management Assistance Team known as FCMAT published its annual audit report on Thursday digging into the district’s finances and facility management.

James Morris the district’s county administrator said the district met every baseline standard.

“I am the happiest guy in the world” Morris said. “This community has been working for 14 years. That success belongs to the people who are here and who stuck with this district.”

Morris said the district needs only to clear the same audit next year for the school board to regain voting power.

It’s been more than 20 years since the LA City Council officially named this neighborhood South LA but for some residents it’ll always be South Central.

South Central LA was popularized in television movies and hip-hop culture in the 1980s and 1990s but according to the LA City Council the name carried a stigma after the 1992 uprisings and gang violence and poverty plagued the predominantly Black neighborhood.

Historically the boundaries of South Central LA include the area between the Harbor freeway on the west side Central Avenue to the east Washington Boulevard to the north and Vernon Avenue to the south. For hundreds of thousands of young undocumented immigrants Deferred Action for Childhood Arrivals — better known as DACA — has provided temporary protection from deportation and authorization to legally work in the United States since it was introduced in 2012.

For years renewing DACA was a routine process that often took just a few weeks. This year has been different.

Across LA recipients say renewals are now taking months leaving some unable to work draining savings accounts and forcing them to question their future in the only country many have ever known.

Jose Morales Perez who has lived in LA since he was 4 years old lost his job after his work permit expired while waiting for his renewal. To make ends meet he has pawned family heirlooms and started selling food out of his home while helping care for his mother whose diabetes has left her unable to walk.

Advocates and lawmakers say the delays are unprecedented. The federal government says the slowdown is the result of more extensive vetting of immigrants.

Making art under the name @tewsr he painted the mural for two weeks in August 2022 and took on the project because of the aspirational message it carries especially for young people growing up nearby.

The USC Fisher Museum of Art opened an exhibit Aug. 18 honoring the legacy of legendary architect Paul R. Williams curating his archival drawings and photographs.

He is the first Black architect licensed west of the Mississippi the first known Black member of the American Institute of Architects nationwide and its first Black fellow. He is also the first and only Black architect to receive the institute’s  highest honor the Gold Medal posthumously in 2017.

During a career spanning nearly six decades Williams designed more than 3000 structures making him one of the most prolific and influential architects of his time.

Geraldine last saw her husband three months ago as he was being led away in handcuffs.

Oscar and Geraldine Polanco were separated for nearly three months after he was detained by federal immigration agents at what he thought was a routine green card adjustment appointment.

Oscar was born in Guatemala and Geraldine was from Peru but they met at a church in West Adams. After getting married in 2023 they were building a life together in Lincoln Heights. 

In October he was led away in handcuffs at his appointment. His wife watched him being taken away.

“She broke down” Oscar recalled. “We both did. You feel powerless like your hands are tied and there’s nothing you can do.”

Geraldine said “They told me he just had to see a judge that it would be a week. But when I saw him like that I felt like everything collapsed.”

He spent about a month at the federal immigration detention facility in Adelanto before he was deported to Guatemala.

The two reunited at an airport in Peru.

They embraced in a long hug surrounded by strangers with their suitcases.

“When I saw her I just went out. I wanted to hug her hug her and tell her that everything was fine and that everything will be fine” Oscar said. “And that thank God we are doing well even though many things were lost along the way but always with the attitude that evertyhing was for the better in the future.”

Pershing Square in downtown LA will soon become Biddy Mason Park.

The LA City Council voted Friday to rename Pershing Square after Bridget “Biddy” Mason a formerly enslaved woman who became one of the city’s founders public servants and philanthropists.

The push to rename the square began in 2024 and was championed by then-Councilmember Kevin de León. In July the petition was reinstated and supported by District 14 Councilmember Ysabel Jurado and District 10 Councilmember Heather Hutt.

Born in Mississippi Mason was brought to California as an enslaved woman but successfully petitioned for her freedom in 1856 according to the National History Museums of LA County.

Mason also co-founded First AME Church which still stands more than 150 years later as a cornerstone of Black LA’s faith community as posted on the church’s website.

Jackie Broxton president of the Biddy Mason Charitable Foundation who also spearheaded the name change said “Biddy Mason’s life and legacy sustain our foundation and provide the inspiration for the work we do within the foster care community.”

The proposal to fence MacArthur Park could make the space easier to maintain according to city officials. But residents worry this would drastically change the fabric of the neighborhood. People who live and work near the park understand something needs to be done to address the area’s woes which have turned it into a political punching bag.

But as Los Angeles officials move forward with plans that could place a fence around MacArthur Park — closing it overnight and creating a permanent physical barrier between the green space and the busy neighborhood around it — there’s little consensus among locals that this latest strategy will fix anything.

The park has evolved into a fixture for political commentary often invoked in broader debates over crime homelessness and immigration. Last summer MacArthur Park drew national attention when federal immigration agents entered the park in a high-profile enforcement operation that city leaders and immigrant advocates described as a show of force in a predominantly immigrant neighborhood.

Community engagement measures — including virtual and in-person town halls and surveys — are expected to roll out to gather community input on the design of the fence. The city has not set a date for those meetings.

Every Monday in March @crenshawmile and Nike host weekly track nights at Crenshaw High School. LA Local reporter LaMonica Peters attended the most recent practice on March 16 where dozens of runners — from first-timers to Olympic veterans — showed up to get their run on.

The weekly practices are in preparation for The Crenshaw Mile race on Saturday April 4. This will be the second year of the race and the organizers said they’re expecting about 2000 people to participate in the event.

The Crenshaw Mile is South LA’s USA Track and Field sanctioned and certified 1-mile road race in the historic Crenshaw District for all runners joggers and walkers 6 years old or older according to  the event’s website.

Co-Founder Sharada Maddox who grew up in the Crenshaw District told The LA Local The Crenshaw Mile event was created because it didn’t exist and the community deserved it.

“It was really simple. As Crenshaw Boulevard being one of the most historic boulevards in the world we asked ourselves: ‘Why isn’t there a race in the neighborhood in the district?’ And so just a couple of questions led to another and we decided to put it together” Maddox said.

“I visited the first concentration camp and I remember swearing that if anything like this ever happened in my lifetime I would do something about it” she said. “We are the hope. The community is the hope that’s missing right now.”
Another volunteer Miriam Arghandiwal said her involvement with the coalition is shaped by her background as an Afghan American and former journalist. “I spent three years reporting on the war in Afghanistan” she said. “I’ve lived in a country where I had every freedom and in a country where people had very few. I understand how bad it can get.”

Home Depot denies cooperating with ICE. In previous statements the company has said it does not participate in immigration enforcement and is not notified in advance of operations.

“We’re required to follow all federal and local rules and regulations in every market where we operate” Home Depot said in a statement posted on X.

@berniesanders took the stage at The Wiltern on Wednesday to boost support for the proposed measure that would impose a one-time tax of up to 5% on individuals and trusts with a net worth above $1 billion with most of the revenue dedicated to health care.

The rally was organized by the @seiuuhw which is leading the effort to qualify what it calls the California Billionaire Tax Act for the November ballot.

Union members gathered signatures at the Koreatown venue on Wednesday to place the measure on the ballot. They will need to gather roughly 875000 valid signatures by June 24.

Measure supporters say the tax could generate roughly $100 billion over five years and help offset anticipated federal reductions to Medi-Cal and other safety-net programs. 

Some attendees came from nearby neighborhoods including Miracle Mile. Others traveled from Topanga and out of state.

Backers estimate about 200 California residents would be affected. Revenue would be collected over several years and deposited into a special state fund with 90% dedicated to health care programs and 10% to education and food assistance.

Anja Kranenburg who flew in from Illinois to visit family in LA said she has supported Sanders for years and believes a wealth tax is necessary.

“It needs to be done in legislation to hold them accountable more and stop them from being able to accumulate and hoard all their wealth” she said.

Opponents of the measure claim that billionaires will flee the Golden State if the measure passes taking their tax dollars with them. 

Gov. Gavin Newsom told The New York Times that he would \"do what I have to do to protect the state” and told Politico that the proposed tax could hurt the state's tax base and force vital industries out of California including the tech industry."

London Carter also known as “Mayor of the Dunbar” sat with LA Local reporter LaMonica Peters to explain the significance of what was once the Dunbar Hotel which is now a senior apartment complex in South Central called Dunbar Village.

The Dunbar Hotel was built in 1928 by two Black dentists John and Vada Somerville at the corner of Central Avenue and 42nd Place. The hotel hosted the NAACP’s first convention on the West Coast and some of the most prestigious Black entertainers and leaders of the time according to the National Trust for Historic Preservation.

What is now considered historic South Central would not be what it is today if it were not for the Dunbar Hotel. The success of the hotel allowed other nightclubs and speakeasies to flourish on Central Avenue creating a vibrant nightlife district in Los Angeles — sometimes called the “Little Harlem” of LA — that welcomed everyone.

“The Dunbar is significant. It’s a part of history. This is where we had refuge. Not only Black Americans but Latinos too. We all were together then” Carte told The LA Local. “Everyday I’m saying ‘Wow I stay where Red Foxx lived. Was it in this room?’ So it’s very precious to me.”

Rey the southern sea otter was not expecting to be a mom.

She was found stranded in July 2023 and deemed unfit to return to the wild. She's been living at the @aquariumpacific and recently was introduced to Sunny a pup who was found orphaned on Asilomar State Beach in February. Their bond was immediate.

They're now together as part of the facility’s surrogacy program. It pairs maternal-age female otters with young motherless pups who would otherwise not survive on their own. As a surrogate mom she’s teaching her adopted baby everything she needs to know to fend for herself.

Sunny and Rey cannot be released into the wild. Experts say both are already too used to being around people and lack the survival instincts to make it on their own in the ocean. But they can raise other otters who eventually could return helping sustain the species that was once on the brink of extinction but has since rebounded to a population of about 3000.

Los Angeles is known as the fragmented metropolis 52 sprawling suburbs in search of a city a patchwork culture without a central neighborhood. But Koreatown has always been the place where these disparate identities overlap. 

It’s not just the densest neighborhood west of Manhattan and a spiritual home for the Korean American diaspora but the city’s cultural center an engine for trends and an island of affordability in central Los Angeles where new immigrants and transplants alike find their first jobs and apartments. 

It’s the midpoint between Eastside and Westside friend groups and families; the birthplace of the Korean taco as well as a Thai restaurant franchise beloved by Mexican Central and South Americans; a Oaxacan cultural enclave and an always-open nightlife district ideal for large groups the place in Los Angeles where the word “everyone” comes the closest to meaning just that.

All decisions in the Inglewood Unified School District have gone through one person a state or county administrator for the last 14 years. 

This means nobody from Inglewood — not the school board parents or teachers — has had the authority to make decisions on issues ranging from controversial school closures to teacher pay to safety on campuses. The constant turnover in county administrators hasn’t helped; there have been nine in 12 years according to the current administrator James Morris. 

All of this could change soon though as the district may soon be able to prove it’s out of the fiscal crisis that placed it under state control or receivership. 

But if an audit in February goes well Morris predicts the school district will officially be back under local control in 2027. 

That would be a major milestone but other financial challenges remain. On top of repaying a $29 million loan the district continues to struggle with falling enrollment and chronic absenteeism which inform how much funding the district receives from the state. 

“The issue is we’ve been in receivership longer than any school district in the history of California and the student attrition rate has never been addressed which is the key reason for the fiscal issues” said John Hughes president of the Inglewood Teachers Association.

Thirty people signed up to compete during this summer’s chess tournament. 

Players of all ages and from across  LA —  and even Sweden —  came to LA Ale Works in Hawthorne to play.

The community that shows up is at the heart of why Larry “LJ” Moody started the chess club.

During the pandemic he would regularly get together with a couple of friends to play chess. Then one day his wife encouraged him to find another place to play.

For years Indonesian Muslims in Southern California gathered at the Indonesian Consulate on Wilshire Boulevard for prayer. The congregation transformed a diplomatic space into a temporary spiritual refuge. The arrangement worked but there was always a longing for home.

If you live in Southern California and you’ve never heard of a street takeover you’ve probably heard one: Engines rev tires screech and fireworks explode. These illegal gatherings happen frequently on weekend nights throughout Los Angeles and Orange counties. Cars block major intersections and create space for other drivers to perform reckless maneuvers including burnouts and donuts. Spectators gather around the middle of “the pit” filming cars spinning past with passengers hanging precariously out of windows.

Fueled by a social media feedback loop the phenomenon took off during the pandemic and events can attract hundreds of spectators. The crowds often made up of minors seek out street takeovers to find community. They know the risks which can be deadly.

A USC reporting lab investigation found that local and state law enforcement are well aware that takeovers have surged but they have struggled to curb them. Talk to people who live near popular takeover intersections and you will learn about scarred streets mangled poles looted stores injured bystanders and tragic deaths.

For nearly five decades Kim Dae-soon who recently passed away made Kim’s Home Center a little piece of home for generations of homesick Korean immigrants where they could furnish their homes with familiar things from Korea.

Known to English-speaking customers as Kim’s Home Center the store’s Korean name is 김스전기 (Kim’s Junggi) or “Kim’s Electric” a name that reflects its beginnings as a shop specializing in electrical goods and appliances.

Kim Dae-soon and his wife Kim Kwee-yul opened the store at Koreatown’s VIP Plaza in 1979. Ten years later they moved the store to its current freestanding location at 2940 W. Olympic Blvd. The couple had started small buying goods at swap meets to repair and resell and eventually became skilled at repairing vacuum cleaners before saving enough to open the store.

Kim Dae-soon died Oct. 7 at 91 the store announced on Instagram. His family will lay him to rest on Wednesday Oct. 28.

The LA Local’s Hanna Kang spoke to Kim’s widow and co-founder Kim Kwee-yul about her late husband along with community members about the Koreatown institution. Read what they shared with her at the link in Koreatown Pico Union and Westlake’s bio.

People who have never relied on a food bank before are increasingly walking through the doors of Community Space Food Bank looking for something to eat.

Some tell Community Space Food Bank co-founder Gaines Newborn that their CalFresh benefits have been reduced or ended. Others say they recently lost their jobs and do not know where else to turn.

The food bank typically saw between two and 10 new people a day. Since the beginning of this year Newborn said that number has climbed to about 30 to 40.

That demand is coming as the food bank is dealing with its own financial challenges. Community Space Food Bank is trying to raise $17000 to cover its expenses for the next two months while also working to buy the building where it operates.

The food bank has been open seven days a week for more than two years including through a fire last year. It serves about 150 hot meals a day and about 100 families through its pantry Newborn said.

One of most striking moments of Sunday’s record-breaking halftime show was when @badbunnypr dropped into his casita catching the family inside completely off guard. It was the first time anyone got to see inside the iconic set that first made an appearance last summer in his Puerto Rico residency.

The inside of the Super Bowl casita feels so much like a real loving Latino home because it was brought to life by a real Latino couple. Argentine production designers Federico Laboreau and Maximiliano Pizzi have been taking Hollywood by storm for years designing sets for film television and major live performances. They can now add Bad Bunny’s casita to their portfolio.

The couple also own Fuegos a speakeasy-style wine-bar and eatery in the Exposition Park neighborhood of South LA that makes empanadas sandwiches and asado.

For diehard Bad Bunny fans the casita is instantly recognizable echoing La Casita stage from his “No Me Quiero Ir De Aquí” residency a now-permanent fixture in his visual iconography that at the Super Bowl attracted celebrity guests like Cardi B Jessica Alba and Pedro Pascal.

Looking back Laboreau said the casita was one of the most meaningful experiences in his career.

“Other projects are nice portfolio projects but this one meant a lot not just because it’s the Super Bowl or Benito or the casita but because of the message” he explained. “It felt like I was showing to America that the Latino community has magic has love — and that we can do whatever we want.”

The volunteer group @crosswalksla has painted hundreds of unsanctioned crosswalks across Los Angeles since 2022. In some cases members of the group have been ticketed for graffiti by the city.

Still they’re committed to their work which they consider a necessary quick response in matters of public safety.

On Sunday the group painted two crosswalks near MacArthur Park on 4th Street. They arrived in high-visiblity vests armed with paint buckets traffic cones and caution tape.

Volunteer Bianca Cockrell said the intersections on 4th Street were chosen for a variety of reasons including the fact that some volunteers live in the area.

“A biker was killed here last year so we painted a crosswalk in his honor to acknowledge that this street is very dangerous for people walking or biking and we wanted to address that” Cockrell said Sunday. “Rampart is also extremely busy — this is a crowded intersection with dense apartment buildings heavy traffic and a lot of people — so we wanted to add crosswalks to make it safer.”

This week marked the 123rd anniversary of when the first Korean immigrants arrived in the United States.

The occasion was celebrated in Los Angeles home to the largest population of Korean Americans outside of South Korea amid ongoing immigration raids by the federal government.

Korean American Day observed annually on Jan. 13 traces back to 1903 when the first group of Korean immigrants arrived in Hawaii to work on sugar plantations.

Events recognizing the day took place throughout the week culminating Friday with @asmmarkgonzalez and community leaders who gathered in Koreatown to mark the anniversary. Speakers reflected on the role Korean Americans have played in shaping Los Angeles - from small businesses to culture and civic life.

The anniversary arrived this year as masked agents descended on the region including the Fashion District in downtown Los Angeles in an apparent immigration raid earlier in the week. 

\"Korean American Day is something that celebrates the history of not just Koreatown but what built this country: immigrants"" Gonzalez said. ""We are not going to let ICE try to trample and try to defeat the history that we have made in this area the progress that we are going to make as a community.""

Robert Ahn @kafla1962 president said the immigration raids are affecting all immigrants.

“We find ourselves in the midst of unprecedented immigration raids. And so what it's done to our community has really had a crushing effect on the Koreatown community. It's really something that's affected all immigrant communities"" he said. ""That's certainly been a focus making sure that our community members know their rights ... and do our part to help alleviate a lot of the anxiety and fear that a lot of our immigrant communities are facing.""

A new exhibit “WE THE PEOPLE” opened at LADC Studios in South LA July 2 centering voices stories and artistic expressions of historically marginalized communities.

The exhibit features more than 30 local artists and runs through July 19. It is free to the public.

The project was created through a partnership between Community Coalition (Community Coalition) and Sankofa.org (Sankofa) the Harry Belafonte Legacy Initiative to address who gets to tell America’s stories as the nation marks its 250th anniversary.

“This exhibit is in many ways a love letter to this community who has a rich history in activism” said Glauz Diego Community Coalition’s vice president of narrative and communications.

In a June 26 statement Community Coalition said the exhibition “confronts the legacies of genocide enslavement land theft state violence and neocolonialism while simultaneously celebrating the movements cultures and communities that have continuously fought to transform the nation.”

Gina Belafonte president and CEO of Sankofa.org told The LA Local the exhibit exemplifies the principles of her father actor and activist Harry Belafonte who believed art and activism would bring change to the world.

“He believed that we needed to use art as a tool to educate our audiences to motivate them to activate them” Belafonte said.

Los Angeles County health officials are investigating a localized outbreak of flea-borne typhus in Wilshire Center a dense area that overlaps with Koreatown.

The incident is the second reported typhus outbreak in the county this year and comes less than two months after health officials warned of the first outbreak in Pico Union. Out of seven people who were diagnosed with typhus five were hospitalized and eventually recovered according to health officials.

While the latest outbreak is in Wilshire Center the Department of Public Health says the risk of flea-borne typhus is countywide. The county has reported 109 cases so far this year.

Flea-borne typhus is caused by bacteria spread by infected fleas which can be carried by rats free-roaming cats opossums and other wildlife. People can become infected when flea feces enter cuts or scrapes or come into contact with the eyes. The illness does not spread from person to person.

The Department of Public Health is urging residents including those in Koreatown and surrounding neighborhoods to take steps to reduce their exposure to fleas.

Jonathan Hale has been painting crosswalks at some of the city’s most dangerous intersections for over a year turning neglected streets into quiet acts of protest and prevention. That work led to his arrest last fall on vandalism — a moment caught on video that went viral.

So far the city isn’t pursuing a misdemeanor charge and the incident gave Hale a chance to present his vision for a safer Los Angeles to Mayor Karen Bass’ office. Now he’s proposing an unusual way for the city to make his guerrilla crosswalks legal: permitted painting parties.

“We’re arguing for a legal mechanism. We should be able to permit street closures as if you were permitting a block party and then we can actually do the thing” Hale told The LA Local. “We can make these (crosswalks) while the street is closed. We can add these compliance lines and it would be like some sort of city-sanctioned street art program. We really want this to be like an alley oop for the city.”

In their proposal to the mayor’s office @peoplesvisionzero presents a “block party” model for installing crosswalks led by residents who could follow specific state standards as a low-cost way to address dangerous streets while working with city agencies rather than waiting years for formal infrastructure projects to move forward.

“I think they see the momentum in the moment” Hale said about the city. “We really want this to be like an alley-oop for the city. But I think it’s going to be unbelievably hard. It’s going to require the coordination of so many different bureaucratic organs. But we want to do it.”

The 53rd annual Los Angeles Korean Festival took over Seoul International Park last week marking a full-throated celebration of Korean culture that also reflects just how far the Korean community in Los Angeles has come.

Approximately 300000 people attended the four-day festival according to organizers.

Even though Los Angeles has no shortage of Korean restaurants grocery stores and other businesses the Korean Food and Agricultural Goods Expo at the festival provided shoppers a chance to find regional foods and products brought directly from their homeland.

Along Irolo Street rows of white tents stretched between Olympic Boulevard and San Marino Street with vendors from eight Korean provinces selling regional goods and traditional specialties. The setup was reminiscent of a Korean jangtuh or traditional marketplace. For some vendors the festival gives them an excuse to make the annual trip across the Pacific.

The LA Local’s Hanna Kang spoke to several vendors who made the journey from South Korea along with a few festival attendees. Swipe through to see what they had to say then head to the link in Koreatown Pico Union and Westlake’s bio for the full story and to see more photos from the festival.

Thousands of people gathered at Los Angeles City Hall Saturday to protest ICE and show solidarity with immigrant communities. Demonstrators filled the steps and surrounding plaza waving U.S. and Mexican flags and holding signs that read “ICE out” “We dissent” and “No one is illegal.”

The rally brought together families students and longtime community organizers calling for an end to immigration enforcement practices they say tear families apart and instill fear in immigrant neighborhoods.

“I think it’s important to be here and stand up for everyone who can’t be here today and to show that we’re educated and can protest peacefully” said Cynthia Basulto a demonstrator at LA City Hall. “It’s empowering to see everyone here today it shows that there’s strength in numbers.”

Four years ago Adan Matul was selling a Guatemalan sweet bread called pan de Xela out of a street cart in the San Fernando Valley. Now Matul and his family run El Sabor Auténtico de Xela a Guatemalan restaurant and bakery in Chatsworth.

“Everything we serve here is a reflection of our roots — the dishes our parents cooked what we snacked on the bread we had with our coffee” Matul told The LA Local. “We want our bread and dishes to evoke memories of home the warmth that we felt eating our mothers’ food.” 

The demand that led to El Sabor Auténtico de Xela opening its doors reflects a broader shift in LA. Los Angeles County is now home to the largest population of Guatemalans outside of Guatemala with more than 280000 residents as of 2025 — a roughly 35% increase over the past decade. As the community has grown so has the visibility of its food even as many Central American immigrants face increased immigration enforcement and political pressure.

Growing up Guatemalan American in Los Angeles I know that feeling. For years food from our homeland was hard to find — even in one of the most diverse food cities in the world.

That’s no longer the case.

Across LA dishes like pepián garnachas and tapado are moving from the margins to the mainstream. What was once hidden is now defining neighborhoods.

These five restaurants capture that shift.

By Andrea G. Mendez Ochoa for The LA Local

Pershing Square in downtown LA will soon become Biddy Mason Park.

The LA City Council voted Friday to rename Pershing Square after Bridget “Biddy” Mason a formerly enslaved woman who became one of the city’s founders public servants and philanthropists.

The push to rename the square began in 2024 and was championed by then-Councilmember Kevin de León. In July the petition was reinstated and supported by District 14 Councilmember Ysabel Jurado and District 10 Councilmember Heather Hutt.

Born in Mississippi Mason was brought to California as an enslaved woman but successfully petitioned for her freedom in 1856 according to the National History Museums of LA County.

Mason also co-founded First AME Church which still stands more than 150 years later as a cornerstone of Black LA’s faith community as posted on the church’s website.

Jackie Broxton president of the Biddy Mason Charitable Foundation who also spearheaded the name change said “Biddy Mason’s life and legacy sustain our foundation and provide the inspiration for the work we do within the foster care community.”

Ramonte Means has been the sole provider for his family piecing together part-time jobs as a janitor and a job coach just to make ends meet. Employers keep his hours below full-time so they don’t have to offer benefits so he keeps his income low enough to qualify for Medi-Cal and keep his kids covered too. He’d rather get insurance through an employer but he can’t afford a plan out-of-pocket.

His story is part of a bigger crisis. State and federal cuts could push California’s uninsured rate to nearly 15% by 2030 leaving a health system on the edge and people like Ramonte fighting to hold onto the coverage they have. Over the past year evidentmediaorg and calmatters gained rare access inside St. John’s Community Health in Los Angeles following the human toll through the eyes of doctors and patients on the front lines a warning of what’s coming as the federal government moves to cut Medicaid at this scale for the first time.

California’s primary election day has passed. Now we wait for results on the races for governor Congress and more. What’s taking so long?

Many of you also asked if you will be able to vote in the general election if you missed the primary. You can vote in the November election as long as you are registered to vote by October 19 even if you missed out on the primary.

LA used to jail people for sleeping on the street. A court case changed the city’s lens on homelessness

In the early 2000s unhoused people in Los Angeles could be arrested for sleeping on the street even if they had nowhere else to go.

Shelter beds were outnumbered by the need. 

In 2006 Jones v. City of Los Angeles challenged that approach. The court ruled the Constitution prohibits punishing “an unavoidable consequence of being human and homeless without shelter.”

The case changed how LA approached enforcement. However later rulings have shifted the legal landscape again.

This story examines what changed and what’s at stake today.

Before Brown v. Board of Education Latino families in California challenged school segregation and won.

In Mendez v. Westminster families argued their children were being denied equal education after being sent to separate underresourced schools.

A federal court agreed ruling the practice unconstitutional. The decision helped lead California to end school segregation and shaped the arguments used in Brown years later.                       
                                                                                                                       Earlier this year 90-year-old Sylvia Mendez  —  daughter of the lead plaintiffs — told students why she’s spent decades keeping her family’s story alive: “I wanted the students to know that someone had fought for them and that they had the right to go to any school they wanted to.”  
                                                                                                                         Boyle Heights carries that legacy at Felicitas and Gonzalo Mendez High School named for Sylvia’s parents. A bill to make Sylvia Mendez Day a California holiday is now under consideration in Sacramento.

LA might be on the verge of its biggest government shakeup in 100 years — and most people have no idea it’s happening.

City leaders are debating proposals that could:
🏛️ Expand the City Council from 15 seats to 25
🌳 Double guaranteed funding for parks
🚨 Give City Council more oversight over LAPD
🗳️ Let 16-year-olds vote in local elections

All of it involves rewriting the LA City Charter — basically the rulebook for how the city works.

Much of the current system was written in 1925 when LA’s population was a fraction of the 4 million residents it is today.

Currently council members are deliberating on what recommendations voters will be asked to approve or reject on their November ballots. Check out The LA Local voter guide for more info.

TLDR:

🛠️ The situation: Seniors at the Robinson-Ellsworth apartments (some residents for 40 years) are facing eviction despite having nowhere else to go.

🔁 The loophole: The Ellis Act (1985) allows landlords to evict tenants if they claim to be exiting the rental industry often a precursor to demolishing rent-controlled units for luxury builds.

⚖️ The limbo: The tenants’ official move-out date was April 7 2026 but they remain in their units as the landlords have refused to meet or provide updates.

📈 The statistics: Homelessness among Angelenos aged 65+ has surged by 36% in the last two years.

🤺 The defenders: The LA Tenants Union (LATU) is calling for a “political fight” demanding that seniors and disabled renters be permanently exempt from Ellis Act evictions.

“Oh that’s my name” Karen recalled saying to herself.

It wasn’t until later that night that she could ask her father about it.

How do you think we can ease up traffic to Dodger Stadium? LADOT wants to know! Fans and residents can now weigh in on a survey launched by the LADOT to ease stadium traffic and identify ways for fans to get to the stadium without their cars.

During 81 home games a season lines of cars inching toward the stadium lead to gridlock on local streets in Chinatown Solano Canyon Echo Park and Lincoln Heights. The problem is a simple numbers game — the reigning World Series champs attract an average 50000 fans per game for a parking lot with 16000 spaces.

The traffic study comes as a response to the proposed Los Angeles Aerial Rapid Transit (LA ART) project a 1.2-mile gondola system that would carry fans to the stadium parking lot from the nearby LA State Historic Park. In 2024 LA City Council approved a motion from District 1 Councilmember Eunisses Hernandez to halt any action on the gondola project until LADOT was able to study traffic easing alternatives.  The survey is live until Monday July 13.

It soon settled upon Dixon that not only was her name misspelled on the Nov. 3 ballot but also that the ballots were already in some voters’ hands.

LA Local youth journalists Lakshmi Leon and Nathan Reyes had the opportunity to speak with LA City Council District 9 candidates Estuardo Mazariegos and Jose Ugarte about green spaces or the lack thereof in South LA.

About five out of 10 LA.County residents live within a 10-minute walk of a park but access to green space is not equal across the county according to the LA County Chief Sustainability Office.

While roughly 50% to 63% of residents countywide live within a 10-minute walk of a park that rate drops significantly in low-income and minority communities like South LA where up to 70% of residents lack nearby park access according to the nonprofit Trust for Public Land.

Heather Hutt who represents LA City Council District 10 asked locals on Tuesday to support a new law called the Commercial Tenant Anti-Harassment Ordinance (TAHO).

In a statement released on June 16 Hutt said the ordinance “will protect small independent and minority-owned legacy businesses from predatory displacement intimidation and landlord overreach.”

“We don’t want big corporations to own everything and no small business has an opportunity to grow” Hutt told The LA Local Tuesday. “We want them to be stabilized and TAHO will stabilize the business owners especially small business owners.”

Tyrei Lacy owner of The District by GS restaurant in South LA spoke about the importance of having an ordinance that protects vulnerable small business owners.

Lacy is currently battling an eviction by Fred Leeds Properties in court and believes the 20-year-contract he signed in 2019 has been breached. The LA Local reached out to Fred Leeds Properties for comment multiple times but has not received a response.

“There is no protection” Lacy said during the press conference. “There is nothing that can save us from these predatory actions so TAHO is amazingly important.”

Hutt said the ordinance is now in committee and City Council will continue to explore what the ordinance will entail and how it will be enforced if passed.

Marqueece Harris-Dawson City Council president and Councilmembers Eunisses Hernandez and Ysabel Jurado of council districts 1 and 14 respectively also spoke during the press conference to show their support for the ordinance.

Post:
Walk through Pico Union near Washington Boulevard and Hoover Street and a larger-than-life portrait of former and current Dodger players Julio Urías Dustin May Freddie Freeman Chris Taylor Mookie Betts and Clayton Kershaw takes center stage.

The piece above the former Advance Auto Parts and tire shop bursts with color and energy depicting the 2022 Dodgers’ lineup. While some might not wear the uniform they still remain part of the Dodgers’ legacy.

The portrait depicts the players in various jerseys each painted to closely resemble their real-life likenesses. One wears the colors of the Mexican flag and they are framed by cheering fans against the Los Angeles skyline. The mural incorporates details of the space itself — a motor and a mechanic’s hand — blending naturally into the working-class neighborhood.
“People like that the players look realistic and the crowd and the city are a part of it” Koreatown-based artist Mike “Tewsr” Duncan said. “Everyone understands why it works — it’s all LA based. There’s pieces of the city and the stadium. It encompasses all these things that people know and appreciate.”

Making art under the name @tewsr he painted the mural for two weeks in August 2022 and took on the project because of the aspirational message it carries especially for young people growing up nearby.

“The Dodgers have been a big thing for people in L.A. for a long time” he said. “The people in Pico Union they appreciate it because they love the Dodgers and they know the players too especially the Latino ones. To them it’s like cool — they feel represented. It’s the heart of the city. Areas that see more gang graffiti in general see us doing public art for the community they take a lot of pride seeing something like that in their area.”

For more than five years Gurpreet Singh 42 says he has looked out for the MacArthur Park community—responding to mental health crises and overdoses by administering Narcan or calling 911. Singh an immigrant from India who arrived in the U.S. 11 years ago also makes sure people have food and water and helps connect them to resources available at the park.

“My mama teach me help to each other so I’m learning through my mama and papa” he said explaining why it’s important for him to help people at the park.

After an injury Singh says he lost his job at a café in the MacArthur Park area and became homeless. A police officer later connected him to shelter at Sixth and Alvarado streets. With the help of Christ-Centered Ministries’ Pit Stop program which provides essential supplies Singh now helps distribute Narcan and other hygiene items such as toothpaste deodorant and soap.

An empty lot at the southwest corner of Wilshire Boulevard and Crenshaw Boulevard could soon transform into nearly 200 affordable apartments.

Abode Communities a nonprofit affordable housing developer plan to develop the Koreatown-adjacent project in partnership with Metro which owns the property. The project would include 194 income-restricted apartments and two manager units for households earning between 30% and 60% of area median income.

Construction is projected to begin in 2028 and continue through 2030 with apartments expected to begin leasing around the same time according to the project’s current timeline.

The project will include 69 one-bedroom units 76 two-bedroom units and 49 three-bedroom apartments along with a 6200-square-foot flex-use transit plaza connecting two bus stops a shared community room landscaped open space a community garden play areas and bike facilities.

This November the city of Los Angeles plans to begin building an 8-foot-tall wrought-iron fence around MacArthur Park. Once the fence is in place Los Angeles police officers will sweep the park for encampments and people sleeping there before the gates shut. The Board of Recreation and Park Commissioners approved the plan Thursday.

The park will stay open while the fence is being built. Once construction is finished the gates are expected to close from 10 p.m. to 6 a.m. LAPD officers will patrol the park while it is open. Officials said the fence is not intended to be permanent.

The fence has drawn mixed reactions from residents and community members with some saying it could make the park safer and easier to maintain while others have raised concerns about how it could affect people who use the park.

Recreation and Parks also announced a larger list of changes planned for the park including restoring access through the tunnel connecting the park’s north and south sides improving accessibility and free Wi-Fi.

The 53rd Los Angeles Korean Festival begins on Thursday at Seoul International Park.

The four-day festival is free and takes place through Sunday with festivities planned from 10 a.m. to 10 p.m. Organizers bill the event as the US’s largest Korean festival bringing together musical artists cultural performances food stalls and shopping.

The free festival is meant to be enjoyed by everyone in the community said Yonah Hong Community Relations Director with the festival. “Our festival is inviting for people of all ages all different backgrounds. You don’t have to have money to enjoy the activities that we offer” said Hong who is also a Koreatown resident.

Friends & Family Flea a new market from the team behind Maum Market will make its debut Saturday in Koreatown.

Most of the 24 vendors participating in the first F&F Flea have some connection to Koreatown according to organizer Arnold Byun. Some grew up in the neighborhood some still live there and others have moved away but retain ties to the area. The vendor list includes apparel brands artists jewelry makers beauty and wellness businesses and food vendors.

There will be plenty of food and shopping including “sogeum-bbang” or salt bread tea handmade candles soaps and vintage clothing as well as flash tattoos and burgers and fries from Love Hour. The LA Hwatu-Hanafuda Club will teach visitors about hwatu the Korean deck of playing cards with roots in Japan. The club will also offer $5 tarot card readings.

Friends & Family Flea runs Saturday Sept. 26 from 11 a.m. to 4 p.m. at Un-Other Space 524 S. Western Ave. Admission is free and organizers are asking attendees to RSVP.

MacArthur Park got an unexpected guest Tuesday: Justin Bieber who joined several members of his band for an impromptu performance.

Social media videos show Bieber 32 sitting on the grass playing percussion and singing as people gather around. He performed several songs to a handful of people including his 2025 hit “Yukon” according to videos from the impromptu performance.

A source close to Bieber told E! News that he visited the park to distribute gift cards and other resources to unhoused people. A spokesperson for the singer could not be immediately reached for comment.

Law enforcement officials were quick to take credit for the pop star’s visit while community leaders pointed to the work of local organizations that have been bringing people together at the park.

YouTube show ‘IUSD Unplugged’ shines a spotlight on Inglewood students

LA Local reporter LaMonica Peters was on set of “IUSD Unplugged” the Inglewood school district’s YouTube show that gives students a chance to interview and serve as hosts.

In this latest episode students Saira Moreira and Malachi Coleman discuss the changes they see on their campuses. Saira is a senior at Inglewood High School United and Malachi is a junior at City Honors Preparatory School. Assistant Superintendent Bernadette Lucas served as  the host.

The goal of the show which is taped quarterly is to give people more insight and information about what’s currently happening and how the district is preparing for the future County Administrator James Morris said.

“IUSD Unplugged” premiered back in September and has published two episodes that have included a range of guests from school principals to even Inglewood Mayor James Butts.

Lopez will gather art and stories from residents that will be part of a large canvas mural and also a part of the community altar that’s going to be built for a “Dia de Los Muertos” event on Sunday.

The Dia de Los Muertos event will start at 3:30 p.m. with a procession on Alvarado and Sixth streets led by the Project for the Arts and Dreams of Indigenous Oaxacan Heritage (PADIOXH) in collaboration with the Westlake Theater Community Alliance.

Music Arts & Community Los Angeles (MAC·LA) kicked off the holiday by hosting two hands-on art making workshops led by artist Marelené Nancy Lopez this past Sunday and Monday at the MacArthur Park Bandshell.

Every Monday in March the Crenshaw Mile and Nike host weekly track nights at Crenshaw High School. LA Local reporter LaMonica Peters attended the most recent practice on March 16 where dozens of runners — from first-timers to Olympic veterans — showed up to get their run on.

The weekly practices are in preparation for The Crenshaw Mile race on Saturday April 4. This will be the second year of the race and the organizers said they’re expecting about 2000 people to participate in the event.

The Crenshaw Mile is South LA’s USA Track and Field sanctioned and certified 1-mile road race in the historic Crenshaw District for all runners joggers and walkers 6 years old or older according to  the event’s website.

Co-Founder Sharada Maddox who grew up in the Crenshaw District told The LA Local The Crenshaw Mile event was created because it didn’t exist and the community deserved it.

“It was really simple. As Crenshaw Boulevard being one of the most historic boulevards in the world we asked ourselves: ‘Why isn’t there a race in the neighborhood in the district?’ And so just a couple of questions led to another and we decided to put it together” Maddox said.

It’s not too late to sign up for the race and more information can be found at thecrenshawmile.com.
